title: Error Handling & Information Leakage
summary: How error messages and timing behavior can hand an attacker a map of the system, and what a safe error response looks like instead.

slides.markdown:
An error message is meant to help — a developer debugging, or a user understanding what went wrong. But a *detailed* error message helps whoever's on the other end of the request equally well, and if that's an attacker, you've just handed them information they didn't have to work for.

This topic is about the gap between **useful for debugging** and **safe to show externally** — a stack trace, a database error, or even how long a request took can each independently leak information about your system's internals, and each needs a deliberate decision about what's shown where, not a default of "just show what happened."

slides.sectionTitle: Why detailed errors help an attacker map your system
slides.markdown:
A detailed error response tells an attacker things they otherwise have to guess or probe for: what language and framework you're running (a stack trace's file paths and function names), what database engine and version you use (a raw SQL error message), what internal file paths exist on the server, and sometimes exact library versions — which then narrows down exactly which known CVEs are worth trying.

This is **reconnaissance for free**. An attacker probing a login form who gets back "invalid password" for a wrong password and a completely different, generic error for a nonexistent username has just learned which usernames exist in your system — without needing to break anything. Multiply that across every endpoint that returns detailed, differentiated errors, and the aggregate leak across a whole application can be a near-complete map of its internals, assembled one small detail at a time.

slides.sectionTitle: Stack traces and debug pages left on in production
slides.markdown:
Most web frameworks ship a **debug mode** that renders a full stack trace, local variable values, and sometimes the exact source code line that failed, directly in the browser when an unhandled exception occurs — genuinely useful during local development, where only the developer sees it.

The recurring, damaging mistake is shipping that same debug mode to production, usually because a configuration flag defaults to "on" and nobody explicitly flipped it off before deploying. The result: any unhandled error in production renders a full stack trace to whoever triggered it, including — depending on the framework — snippets of source code, file system paths, and sometimes even values of local variables that can include secrets or session data.

This is one of the most consistently found issues in real-world security scans specifically because it's a single configuration flag, easy to forget, with a blast radius as large as "every unhandled exception in the entire application, forever, until someone notices."

slides.sectionTitle: Generic user-facing errors vs detailed internal logs
slides.markdown:
| | User-facing response | Internal log |
|---|---|---|
| Detail level | Generic — "Something went wrong, try again" | Full — stack trace, request context, variable state |
| Audience | Anyone who sent the request, including a possible attacker | Engineers with access to the logging system |
| Purpose | Doesn't help debug; only needs to not leak anything | The actual debugging resource |
| Correlation | A generic error should still include a request/error ID | That same ID lets an engineer find the matching detailed log entry |

The pattern that satisfies both goals at once: return a generic message plus a **correlation ID** (a random identifier unique to that specific error occurrence) to the caller, and log the full detail — stack trace, request parameters, everything useful — internally under that same ID. Support or engineering can then look up the exact failure using the ID the user reports, without any of that detail ever having been exposed in the response itself.

slides.subTitle: When "how long it took" leaks information
slides.markdown:
Even a perfectly generic error message can leak information through a side channel: **how long the server took to respond.** If checking a username involves a database lookup that fails fast for a nonexistent user but a full password comparison for an existing one, a login endpoint that returns the identical error message for both cases can still be distinguished by an attacker simply by measuring response time — a slower response reveals a valid username exists, even though the message text gives away nothing.

This matters most in comparison operations: a naive string comparison of a submitted token against a stored secret typically returns as soon as it finds the first mismatched character, so the comparison takes measurably longer the more leading characters match — an attacker can, in principle, guess a secret one character at a time by measuring which guess takes slightly longer.

The fix for the comparison case is a **constant-time comparison** function (most languages provide one specifically for secrets/tokens) that always takes the same amount of time regardless of where or whether a mismatch occurs. The fix for the broader "different code paths take different times" case is harder and often means deliberately equalizing the work done on both paths, or adding a randomized or fixed delay to mask the difference.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: how fast leaked errors get found
slides.markdown:
Automated web vulnerability scanners specifically probe for information disclosure as a routine, cheap check — sending malformed input to every discoverable endpoint and inspecting the response for stack traces, database error strings, or framework version banners. This kind of scanning is fast and untargeted: a scanner can check hundreds of endpoints for this class of issue in the time it would take a human to manually test one, and it requires no specific vulnerability knowledge, just pattern-matching on error output.

The practical consequence: a debug-mode-enabled production deployment or a verbose error handler isn't a needle in a haystack that only a sophisticated, targeted attacker would find — it's one of the first things almost any automated scan or opportunistic attacker checks for, which is exactly why it shows up so often in penetration test findings as a "quick win" for the tester, and why it's worth fixing before worrying about more exotic vulnerability classes.

slides.sectionTitle: Consistent error behavior as a design discipline
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
The subtlety that goes beyond "hide the stack trace": information leakage through errors is rarely one dramatic mistake, it's usually **inconsistency** across many small decisions — one endpoint returns a generic error while a similar one on a different team's service still returns a raw database exception, one comparison uses a constant-time function while a similar check elsewhere in the codebase uses a naive one written before anyone thought about timing.

A mature approach treats "what does an error response look like" as a **platform-level concern**, not a per-endpoint judgment call: a shared error-handling middleware or framework convention that every endpoint gets by default, so an individual engineer doesn't have to remember to sanitize every exception by hand. This is the same structural-enforcement pattern that shows up across this entire area — moving a security property from "something every engineer must remember" to "something the platform enforces by default" is consistently the stronger design, and error handling is one of the easiest places to apply it because the correct behavior (generic message, correlation ID, detailed internal log) is the same for almost every endpoint.

slides.sectionTitle: Returning a full stack trace in an API's JSON error body
slides.markdown:
The pitfall, very concretely: an API's error handler catches an unhandled exception and, rather than mapping it to a generic response, serializes the exception object directly into the JSON error body — stack trace, exception type, sometimes even the internal exception message from a database driver, all returned to the caller verbatim.

This is functionally identical to leaving debug mode on, just scoped to APIs rather than server-rendered pages, and it's a common gap specifically because it's easy to write a catch-all handler that does `return {"error": str(exception)}` as a quick fix during development and never revisit it before shipping — it *works*, in the sense that it returns something, so nothing forces a second look.

The fix: a catch-all error handler should map any unhandled exception to a fixed, generic response structure (message plus correlation ID) and log the actual exception detail server-side — never serialize an exception object, or its string representation, directly into a response body that leaves the system, regardless of how convenient that was during development.
